name: eGFR and creatinine: kidney test results
summary: Creatinine and eGFR show how well the kidneys filter blood, and kidney disease is confirmed only when abnormal results persist.
keyPoints: Creatinine is a waste product measured in the blood, and eGFR is an estimate of kidney filtering worked out from it.
As kidney function declines, the eGFR may fall over time.
One abnormal result is not enough to diagnose chronic kidney disease, which is confirmed when eGFR stays low over about three months.
A urine test, the albumin to creatinine ratio, is used alongside eGFR because it can show kidney damage.

body.heading: What are creatinine and eGFR?
body.body: Creatinine is a waste product, and the blood test measures how much of it is in the blood. The eGFR, or estimated glomerular filtration rate, is calculated from the creatinine result. The calculation also takes account of age and sex. Lab Tests Online UK explains that the eGFR may fall over time as kidney function declines. Because eGFR comes from a routine blood test, it lets clinicians spot kidney problems before symptoms appear. People with more muscle naturally make more creatinine, which can give a lower eGFR than their kidney function really is. Cystatin C is another marker filtered by the kidneys and is less affected by muscle mass than creatinine.

body.heading: What does a low eGFR mean?
body.body: A low eGFR may be a sign of kidney disease, though a single result is not enough to say. NICE says testing for chronic kidney disease uses both an eGFR and a urine ACR. A slightly raised urine ACR, which checks for the protein albumin, may indicate early-stage kidney disease. eGFR falls naturally with age, which does not always mean kidney disease. The estimate is unreliable when kidney function is changing quickly, as in acute kidney injury.

body.heading: How is chronic kidney disease confirmed?
body.body: One abnormal result is not enough. A diagnosis is usually confirmed only if repeated eGFR tests are consistently lower than normal over about three months. NICE says a low first eGFR should be repeated soon, to check whether sudden kidney injury is the cause. The urine albumin to creatinine ratio, or ACR, compares albumin with creatinine in a urine sample. Alongside the eGFR, urine tests give a more accurate picture of how well the kidneys are working. Results are classed by eGFR category and by ACR category, which together show the stage. Lab Tests Online UK says a very high urine ACR shows that kidney disease is present in a more severe form.

body.heading: Who is tested?
body.body: Testing is recommended for people with risk factors such as diabetes, high blood pressure, past acute kidney injury or cardiovascular disease. Early chronic kidney disease often causes no symptoms, so it is commonly found through routine blood or urine tests. Later symptoms can include tiredness, swollen ankles, feet or hands, shortness of breath, blood in the urine and passing urine more often at night. The NHS advises seeing a GP about symptoms that persist.

body.heading: What are the limits of the test?
body.body: Creatinine-based eGFR may be less reliable in older adults. In that situation another marker, cystatin C, can help. Creatinine can also be influenced by factors other than the kidneys, such as how much muscle a person has. NICE advises that the urine ACR is ideally measured on an early morning sample.

body.heading: What happens after a diagnosis?
body.body: Chronic kidney disease is most often caused by damage from other conditions, most commonly diabetes and high blood pressure. There is no cure, but care can slow progression. Kidney function is monitored with regular blood and urine tests. Care centres on blood pressure control, managing diabetes, prescribed medicines, diet advice and not smoking. The NHS says medicines can help control related problems and keep the kidneys working for longer. The NHS says most people with chronic kidney disease can control the condition with medicine and regular check-ups. Glomerulonephritis, inflammation of the filters inside the kidneys, is another cause of kidney disease.

body.heading: How often are kidney tests repeated?
body.body: NICE guideline NG203 says the monitoring frequency it recommends is a minimum, and that more frequent monitoring may suit some people. NICE sets a minimum number of checks each year, which depends on the eGFR and ACR categories. It also reflects how quickly the eGFR or ACR is changing and other conditions such as diabetes. NICE says ACR monitoring should be individualised, for example more often when the ACR is higher. NICE lists diabetes among the risk factors for which eGFR and ACR testing is advised.
